entities.summary:
The Hephthalites, a powerful nomadic confederation often referred to as the 'White Huns' (though their ethnic link to the Huns of Europe is debated), emerged as a dominant force in Central Asia from approximately 408 CE until the 560s CE. Their vast, mobile empire spanned an immense territory, encompassing modern-day Afghanistan, parts of Central Asia (including Transoxiana and Bactria), and extending into the Indian subcontinent. They are primarily significant for their profound disruption of the Sasanian Persian Empire and their instrumental role in the collapse of the Gupta Empire in India, fundamentally altering the political and cultural landscape of these regions during Late Antiquity.

Operating from their strongholds in Bactria and Tokharistan, the Hephthalites engaged in a series of devastating conflicts. Their military prowess was demonstrated most notably in 484 CE, when they decisively defeated and killed the Sasanian Shah Peroz I at the Battle of Herat, inflicting a crippling blow that forced the Sasanian Empire into decades of tribute payments and internal instability. Concurrently, Hephthalite incursions into India, beginning in the late 5th century under leaders such as Toramana and Mihirakula, systematically dismantled the once-mighty Gupta Empire, leading to its fragmentation into numerous smaller kingdoms and profoundly influencing the subsequent course of Indian history.
